lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In the spring of 1943, a Harvard chemist stood on a brand-new American airfield and armed six sleeping bats with tiny firebombs, while Army cameramen filmed him doing it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The desert sun woke the bats up before anyone had planned for it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Exactly fifteen minutes later, the barracks caught fire. Then the control tower went up like a giant candle. Then the offices, and then the hangars, one after another, in the order he had armed the bats.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The fire trucks raced to the gate, and the guards refused to open it, because the whole thing was top secret.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: To understand how six bats beat the United States Army, we have to go back to a dentist.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Then the radio told him about Pearl Harbor.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Most people heard that news and felt fear, or anger. Doc Adams looked at the bats.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Years later he described the moment himself. He had been, in his words, "tremendously impressed by the bat flight," and he wondered: "Couldn't those millions of bats be fitted with incendiary bombs and dropped from planes?"

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It opened gently. The bat, Adams wrote, was "the lowest form of life," and the reasons for its creation had always remained a mystery, until now. Bats, he explained, had been "placed there by God to await this hour."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Franklin Roosevelt read it, and passed it to his intelligence chief, William Donovan, with a note that still survives: "This man is not a nut. It sounds like a perfectly wild idea but is worth looking into."

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: That's the reference? "Not a nut"?

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: From the President. Most of us can't get that from our own families.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Armed with that note, Adams went recruiting. His team included a mammal scientist from a Los Angeles museum, a high-school student named Jack Couffer, who had turned seventeen on the day of Pearl Harbor, a lobster fisherman, and a man who had driven getaway cars for the mob.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Couffer later admitted that Adams "chose them more for personality than technical expertise."

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: So the team is a dentist, a toy company and Bing Crosby.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And Harvard. To keep it serious.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Fieser later wrote, "We were horrified to find that Adams had invited a large company, including ladies, to a dinner party in celebration of the initiation of field tests."

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: He threw a party. For the secret weapon.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: It was very secret. Only the guests knew.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Fieser worked out why. "Instead of freezing them to hibernation, we had frozen them to death the night before."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The base commander, a full colonel, agreed to delay opening his own airfield for the secret project. The lieutenant colonel running the test then barred him from watching, for secrecy. Still not a nut, technically.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: He had. "Like bats flyin' 'round in broad daylight? Unusual like that?"

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: They begged him to keep it secret. He had two sons fighting in Europe, he told them, and nobody would get a word out of him, "even by puttin' bamboo splinters under my fingernails."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The delivery system worked.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That's when the New Mexico sun woke the bats up.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Couffer remembered exactly what happened next: "Exactly fifteen minutes after arming, a barracks burst into flames; minutes later the tall tower erupted into a huge candle visible for miles."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Once the fires had burned out, the officer in charge asked the commander if he could borrow a bulldozer, to flatten whatever was left.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Some accounts say even a general's car caught fire. The Army's official report summed up the day in one sentence: testing was concluded "when a fire destroyed a large portion of the test material."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: That's one way to describe an airfield.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: Two years, two million dollars, it finally works, and that's when they cancel it.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The bats were always right on time. The paperwork wasn't.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Doc Adams never really understood why. Couffer later remembered Adams coming back from Washington, baffled, because a general had mixed up their secret project with another one he'd never heard of. Adams called it "the silliest nonsense you ever heard of."

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The other project was the atomic bomb.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Roosevelt had been right, in the end. Doc Adams was not a nut. He was something far more dangerous: a cheerful man with a letter from the President in his briefcase.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: The idea of burning Japan's wooden cities didn't end with the bats. In March 1945, American bombers firebombed Tokyo with ordinary incendiaries. In a single night, about a hundred thousand people were killed.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: After years of trying to drop fire from the sky, he'd finally found something to drop that grew instead of burned.
